title: Social Security Design and Its Political Support
text:
About this appendix
This online appendix accompanies Social Security Design and Its Political Support by Rasmus K. S. Berg and Martín Gonzalez-Eiras. It holds the tables and figures behind the paper’s quantitative sections, the robustness checks that the paper’s appendix G summarizes in one figure, and the numerical checks behind its results, with each figure set beside the tables that print its numbers. Every exhibit is built by the paper’s own pipeline from the model’s results, so the numbers are the paper’s to the last printed digit; replication lists where each one comes from.
Reading an exhibit. Point at a marker of a figure to read its value; click it to bring up the table that prints it, with its row highlighted. Point at a table row to find its markers in the figure. Where an exhibit exists under both calibrations of the households’ taste for leisure, a switch moves between the paper’s calibration, common \(X\), and the alternative, vector \(X_i\) (OA.3.2), and mark the cells that differ shows which numbers the choice moves. The address in the browser keeps the selection, so a link opens the same table and row. Under Source, each exhibit lists the files it reads, with downloads, the builder that makes it and the command that rebuilds it. A grey badge marks an exhibit of the paper itself; every other exhibit is numbered here, Table or Figure OA.k.
The print edition, a PDF under the download link of the sidebar, holds every table and figure that is not in the paper, with the same numbers.

title: Social Security Design and Its Political Support
text:
Robustness at a glance
Figure G.1 of the paper, repeated here, sets its quantitative results against every specification the paper reports. Each panel is one result: how the tax rate responds to the Bismarckian index \(\theta\), to acute ageing and to France’s income distribution and voting patterns with the design given, and how the chosen design responds to the last three. Each marker is the same result under one specification: the intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES) \(\rho\), the calibration of the taste for leisure, the host economy, and for the chosen design the cost specification and the Frisch elasticity \(\xi\). Results are changes against the host’s own baseline at the same IES, and the paper’s own reading, the U.S. under a common \(X\) at an IES of one with the cost of section 7, is the highlighted marker. Click a marker for the table that prints it.
\(\cdot\)



Figure G.1 of the paper: a marker across the zero line from the highlighted one reverses the paper’s sign. With the design given, the Beveridgean corner against the Bismarckian one, acute ageing and France’s voting patterns raise the tax rate in every specification; France’s income distribution lowers it on the U.S., and on the UK raises it under a common \(X\) and lowers it under the vector \(X_i\). With the design chosen, acute ageing makes the design more Bismarckian and France’s voting patterns less so throughout, while France’s income distribution moves it in a direction that changes with the IES and the host, and to the Bismarckian corner under the cost on the design.

title: OA.1 The cross-section of figure 1.1
text:
OA.1.1 Countries, values and sources
Figure 1.1 of the paper sets pension spending and the Bismarckian–Beveridgean index of the OECD countries against their population growth and their income inequality. This chapter gives the values behind each marker, the year each refers to, the sources, and the correlations the paper’s introduction describes.
Point at a marker to see which country it is. The table of countries prints every variable the figure draws, with the year of each value; the table of sources names, for every column, the provider, the dataset and the series, and when it was retrieved.
\(\cdot\)

title: OA.1 The cross-section of figure 1.1
text:
Figure 1.1 of the paper: one marker per country, with the three economies the paper calibrates labeled. The Bismarckian–Beveridgean index is the ratio of the gross replacement rates for men at mean and at half-mean earnings: one where benefits are proportional to earnings, one half where they are flat. Pension spending and the index both fall as population growth rises, and neither has a clear relation to the Gini coefficient (table OA.3).In the paper · figure 1.1, section 1 Population growth, title: OA.2 Argentina
text:
OA.2.1 Calibration
Section 5 of the paper calibrates the model with informal households to Argentina before the coverage reforms and reads the reforms as a rise of the universal pension \(\epsilon\); appendix E gives the survey, the identifying formulas and the sources. This chapter holds the calibration under both treatments of the taste for leisure, the reform at every intertemporal elasticity of the model’s grid, the equilibrium over pension designs, and the calibration at every IES.
The paper takes the taste for leisure common to the four formal quartiles and pins its level by the average formal workweek, so relative hours are a prediction. The alternative identifies one \(X_i\) per quartile from the survey’s relative hours. Only the productivity and leisure parameters differ between the two: the aggregate targets, and every result of section 5, are the same under both.
\(\cdot\)

title: OA.2 Argentina
text:
OA.2.2 The reform
The first table is the paper’s: the effect in 2010 of raising \(\epsilon\) to the universal level, with the tax rate held at its pre-reform path and chosen politically. The second prints the paths of the tax rate, the savings rate and the workweek before and after the reform.
\(\cdot\)


Calibrationcommon X (the paper’s)vector Xi Mark the cells that differ from the other calibration

Table 2 of the paper: the effect in 2010 of raising the universal pension \(\epsilon\) to the level at which informal retirees receive the benefit of the least productive formal workers, unanticipated and permanent. The first row is the pre-reform economy; the second holds the tax rate at its pre-reform path and so isolates the response of households; the third lets the electorate reset the tax. Taxes rise, because the reform moves benefits toward informal retirees, who are poorer than formal ones and value them more at the margin, and savings and hours fall a little; with the tax held fixed, formal savings rise instead, since informal households now hold a claim on the system and save less.Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this exhibit is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so the aggregates the reform moves do not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the quartiles.The same reform along the path: the tax rate, the savings rate and the workweek in every model period from the reform year on, on the pre-reform path and on the reform path side by side. The tax response builds over the first periods, because informal households, now covered, save less for retirement and as retirees demand more taxation; section 5 of the paper quotes the response one period on.Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this exhibit is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so the aggregates the reform moves do not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the quartiles.

OA.2.3 The reform across the intertemporal elasticity
Section 5 reads the reform across the intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES) \(\rho\) from the figure, which is the paper’s; the model is solved on a grid of sixteen values. The table prints the reform at every point of the grid. Click a point of the figure for its row.
\(\cdot\)


Calibrationcommon X (the paper’s)vector Xi Mark the cells that differ from the other calibration

Figure 5.2 of the paper: the effect of the reform on the tax rate, the savings rate, the workweek and the ratio of informal to formal savings, on impact and one period on, at every IES of the grid, each economy recalibrated to the same pre-reform targets. Below an IES of one the responses are dampened, and at the lowest elasticities the tax response on impact reverses, since the young resist taxation more and the calibration needs a heavier political weight of the old to reproduce the observed tax rate; between one and two the responses stay close to the log benchmark.Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this exhibit is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so the aggregates the reform moves do not depend on how the taste for text:
OA.2.4 The equilibrium over pension designs
The equilibrium in 2010 over a grid of designs \((\epsilon, \theta)\), each point an economy that has always had that design, with the pre-reform calibration and the universal system at the calibrated \(\theta\) marked. The tax rate rises with \(\epsilon\) and falls with \(\theta\), the savings rate and the workweek fall with \(\epsilon\) and rise with \(\theta\), and the savings of informal relative to formal households fall with \(\epsilon\). Between the two markers the tax rate rises by more than it does on impact in section 5 of the paper, because the savings of informal households have adjusted to the universal system; the difference is close to the reform’s effect by 2040 (OA.2.2). The grid itself can be downloaded from the figure’s source.

OA.2.5 The calibration across the intertemporal elasticity
The table and the figure print the parameters solved jointly with the equilibrium path at every IES of the grid, which show how the calibration absorbs a change in \(\rho\): matching the targets at an IES of 0.6 or below takes a thirty-year discount factor above one.
\(\cdot\)


Calibrationcommon X (the paper’s)vector Xi Mark the cells that differ from the other calibration

Four panels are parameters solved at each IES and two are predictions of the calibration, the savings rate and the informal savings ratio in 2010. The discount factor and the political weight of the old both fall as the IES rises, the second because the young resist taxation less and a lighter weight of the old reproduces the observed tax rate; the savings rate falls, the informal savings ratio rises, and the informal productivity and taste for leisure barely move.Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration the discount factor, the political weight of the old, the savings rate and the informal savings ratio are those of the common \(X\) at every IES; only the informal productivity and taste for leisure take other values, and they too barely move with the IES.Figure OA.4 The Argentine calibration across the intertemporal elasticity

title: OA.3 The rich economies with the design given
text:
OA.3.1 Calibration
Section 6 of the paper calibrates the model without informal households to the U.S., France and the UK, and changes the U.S. calibration one characteristic at a time, its pension design, its demography and the characteristics that set France apart; appendix F gives the data and the household heterogeneity behind the calibration. This chapter holds every table behind section 6’s figure, the counterfactuals under CRRA preferences and the same counterfactuals with the UK as host, each under both calibrations of the taste for leisure, and the calibrations at every intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES) of the model’s grid.
The first table prints the country parameters, with those the three countries share in a lower panel; the others print, by income group, the population shares, the taste for leisure, the productivities and the propensities to vote. France is grouped at the U.S. income percentiles and, for the UK as host, at the UK’s. The UK is also regrouped at the U.S. percentiles for one row of the paper’s cross-country test in section 7; that regrouping is a linear fit of the UK’s own group means against their cumulative population shares, not a recount of the survey.
\(\cdot\)

text:
OA.3.2 The vector-\(X_i\) calibration
The paper identifies each income group’s productivity and taste for leisure by taking the taste for leisure common across groups and fixing its level by the average workweek, so that relative hours are a prediction. The alternative takes the observed relative hours as data as well, which identifies one \(X_i\) per group and leaves the level of hours unidentified. The productivity distribution reaches every aggregate only through \(\sum_i \gamma_i \eta_i^{1+\xi}/X_i^{\xi}\), which both calibrations normalize to one, so the calibration is block recursive: what depends on the design or on the demography is the same under both, exactly in the log case and, in the CRRA solves for the UK and France, to within one unit of the last printed digit, and only what is defined through \(\eta_i\) or \(X_i\) separately can move. The table compares every exhibit that exists under both calibrations, cell by cell, the Argentine exhibits of OA.2 included; on each exhibit, the calibration switch and mark the cells that differ show the same comparison in place.

OA.3.3 The calibration across the intertemporal elasticity
The figure and the table print the parameters solved jointly with the equilibrium path at every IES of the grid, for each country. Sections 6 and 7 explain the CRRA results by how the calibration absorbs a higher IES; these are the numbers behind that explanation. Matching the U.S. targets at an IES of 0.6 or below takes a thirty-year discount factor above one, which the UK and France inherit.
\(\cdot\)


Calibrationcommon X (the paper’s)vector Xi Mark the cells that differ from the other calibration

One line per country; the discount factor is the U.S. one in all three. The political weight of the old falls as the IES rises in every country, since the young resist taxation less, and keeps its ranking, highest in the U.S. and lowest in the UK; the savings rate falls in every country, and the interest factor of the UK and France, a prediction, rises toward the U.S. target.Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration there is no common taste for leisure to draw, and every text:
OA.3.4 Counterfactuals on the U.S.
The paper’s overview figure of section 6 collects the effect of each counterfactual on the tax rate, the savings rate and the workweek at three values of the IES. Each counterfactual is a separate equilibrium path read in 2020: one characteristic of the U.S. calibration is changed over the whole horizon and every other parameter, the political weight of the old included, stays at its U.S. value, so a row describes an economy that has always had that characteristic. The tables print the effects: the pension design and ageing at the paper’s benchmark, with the economic-equilibrium effect, in which the tax rate is held at its baseline path, beside the full one; France’s income distribution, leisure preferences and voting patterns one at a time and all at once, next to France’s own calibrated path; and the same counterfactuals at each IES. Click a bar for its row.
\(\cdot\)


Calibrationcommon X (the paper’s)vector Xi Mark the cells that differ from the other calibration

Figure 6.1 of the paper: one row per characteristic changed in the U.S. calibration, at three values of the IES. The design and ageing dominate the tax panel at an IES of one or below, while at an IES of two France’s voting patterns move the tax rate by more than the whole range of the design. France’s leisure preferences dominate the workweek panel and leave the tax and savings rates essentially unchanged.Only the rows that impose France’s productivities or its taste for leisure differ from the paper’s figure: France’s income distribution lowers the tax rate and lengthens the workweek by more at every IES, and its leisure preferences shorten the workweek a little less. The rows for the design, ageing and voting patterns are the paper’s.In the paper · figure 6.1, section 6 The effect of various counterfactuals in the U.S.

The design at its two corners against the observed one, at an IES of one. Moving to flat benefits raises the tax rate and lowers the savings rate and the workweek; with the tax held at its baseline path it raises the savings rate instead, so the tax response is what lowers it, while for hours the two effects point the same way. Fully earnings-related benefits reverse every sign.Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this table is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so what the design and the demography move does not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the income groups.The two ageing scenarios at an IES of one. Ageing raises the tax rate and lowers the savings rate and the workweek, acute ageing by more than mild; with the tax held at its baseline path the savings rate does not move and the workweek lengthens, so both falls come from the tax response.Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this table is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so what the design and the demography move does not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the income groups.France’s characteristics on the U.S. at an IES of one. France’s income distribution lowers the tax rate and raises the savings rate and the workweek, its voting patterns raise the tax rate, and its leisure preferences shorten the workweek and move nothing else. All three together bring the workweek close to France’s but move the tax rate away from it.Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration only the rows that impose France’s productivities or its taste for leisure differ: France’s income distribution lowers the tax rate and raises the savings rate by more, alone and with the other characteristics, and the workweek is longer in each of these rows. Every sign is that of the common \(X\), and the voting row and France’s own path are unchanged.The design at its two corners at each IES. Flat benefits raise the tax rate and shorten the workweek at every IES and fully earnings-related ones do the reverse, both by less the higher the IES, since the calibration then needs a lower political weight of the old and the difference between rich and poor retirees counts for less. Flat benefits lower the savings rate at \(\rho = 0.5\) and 1 but raise it a little at \(\rho = 2\), where both corners raise it.Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this table is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so what the design and the demography move does not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the income groups.The two ageing scenarios at each IES. Ageing raises the tax rate and lowers the savings rate and the workweek at every IES, acute ageing by more than mild, and the tax response falls only a little as the IES rises, where that of the design falls steeply (table OA.27).Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration this table is identical to the common-\(X\) one to the last printed digit, as the comparison in section OA.3.2 records: the calibration is block recursive, so what the design and the demography move does not depend on how the taste for leisure is split across the income groups.France’s characteristics on the U.S. at each IES. The income distribution lowers the tax rate at every IES and the voting patterns raise it, the first by less and the second by more the higher the IES, and the leisure preferences move essentially the workweek alone. With all three together the tax rate falls at \(\rho = 0.5\) and 1 and rises at \(\rho = 2\), where the voting patterns prevail.Under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration only the rows that impose France’s productivities or its taste for leisure differ: the income distribution lowers the tax rate by more at every IES, and with all three characteristics together the tax rate falls at every IES, only marginally at \(\rho = 2\), where under the common \(X\) it rises. title: OA.3 The rich economies with the design given
text:
OA.3.5 The UK as host
The counterfactuals of section 6 on the UK’s own calibration, each a separate equilibrium path with one characteristic changed over the whole horizon and every other parameter at the UK’s value: France’s characteristics, with France’s households regrouped at the UK’s income percentiles, and the pension design and ageing at each IES. The figure sets the two hosts side by side for France’s characteristics; the tables print the UK’s numbers. Two differences from the U.S. stand out. France’s income distribution raises the UK’s tax rate where it lowers the U.S. one, because at the UK’s income cuts France is the more unequal of the two countries (OA.3.1) and equilibrium taxes rise with inequality; and France’s taste for leisure lengthens the UK’s workweek where it shortens the U.S. one, since France’s average taste for leisure lies between the two hosts’. France’s voting profile raises the tax rate on both hosts, by more at a higher IES. The income-distribution row is also the one that depends on the calibration of the taste for leisure: under the vector-\(X_i\) calibration it lowers the UK’s tax rate, because that calibration reads part of the observed income dispersion off relative hours, which are much flatter in the UK than in France.

title: OA.4 The endogenous pension design
text:
OA.4.1 The cost and the cross-country test
Section 7 of the paper lets the electorate choose the design \(\theta\) as well as the tax rate, under a deadweight cost of redistribution whose parameter \(\lambda\) is calibrated so that the U.S. electorate re-elects its observed design. This chapter holds the tables behind section 7, the same counterfactuals with the UK as host, the design along the baseline path, the timing of the choice and an alternative cost specification.
The paper’s two tables of section 7.2: the calibrated cost at each intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES), and the designs the UK and France choose under the U.S. parameter, with the UK’s own parameter; France, at the corner, has none.
\(\cdot\)
crumbs: 4  OA.4 The endogenous pension design

title: OA.4 The endogenous pension design
text:
Table 4 of the paper: one row per IES, each with the cost parameter at which the U.S. electorate re-elects its observed design in 2020. The parameter, and with it the share of revenue lost at the observed design and at flat benefits, falls steeply as the IES rises, since a higher elasticity strengthens the forward-looking channels that hold the choice away from the Beveridgean corner.Table 5 of the paper: the test of the cost parameter calibrated on the U.S. alone, at an IES of one. Under the U.S. parameter the chosen designs keep the observed ranking of the UK, the U.S. and France, compressed toward the U.S. value; the UK’s own parameter lies below the U.S. one, and regrouping the UK at the U.S. income percentiles moves its chosen design only slightly.

OA.4.2 Counterfactuals on the U.S.
Each counterfactual is a separate equilibrium path read in 2020, with one characteristic changed over the whole horizon, every other parameter at its U.S. value and the political choice binding from the first period. Each is read twice, with the design pinned at the U.S. value and with the design chosen, and both readings carry the cost, so the distance between them is the political response. The figure’s last row, France’s income distribution and voting patterns together, shares its design, tax rate and savings rate with the table’s row that imposes all French characteristics, since France’s level of \(X\) moves hours and nothing else. In the paper’s figure an open marker is the pinned reading and a filled one the chosen; click either for its row.
\(\cdot\)



Figure 7.1 of the paper: each counterfactual with the design pinned and with it chosen, at three values of the IES. Acute ageing moves the chosen design toward earnings-related benefits and France’s voting patterns toward flat ones at every IES, the voting patterns furthest at \(\rho = 2\), where choosing the design also adds to the rise in the tax rate and shortens the workweek; the direction in which France’s income distribution moves the design changes with the IES, and the last row follows the voting title: OA.4 The endogenous pension design
text:
OA.4.3 The UK as host
The same counterfactuals with the UK as host, at the UK’s own cost parameter, the one at which its electorate re-elects the UK’s observed design; it lies below the U.S. parameter at an IES of one or below and above it at two. The figure sets the two hosts side by side; the tables print the UK’s numbers. On both hosts France’s voting profile moves the design most, toward flat benefits, and by less on the UK, whose own voting profile is already flatter than the U.S. one. France’s income distribution moves the two hosts’ designs in opposite directions, since on the U.S. it compresses relative incomes and on the UK it spreads them. The design response leaves the UK’s tax rate, savings rate and workweek essentially at the reading with the design pinned, so on the UK the response is confined to the design itself.
\(\cdot\)



France’s characteristics on the two hosts with the design chosen, the U.S. in the upper row of panels and the UK in the lower, on shared axes so that the hosts compare by position. The last row is France’s income distribution and voting patterns together, whose design and tax rate are those of the tables’ all-French rows. On the U.S. that row follows the voting patterns at every IES; on the UK it does so at \(\rho = 1\) and 2, while at \(\rho = 0.5\) the chosen design barely moves.Figure OA.11 Endogenous pension design OA.4.4 The design along the baseline path
The calibration pins the design in 2020 only; every other design on the path, before 2020 as after it, is an outcome of the model. Section 7 describes the drift of the design along the baseline path in words; here are the paths of the design and of the tax rate, chosen and pinned, at each IES and at two other values of the Frisch elasticity \(\xi\), which the paper reports in a footnote.
\(\cdot\)



Along the baseline path the chosen design dips below the observed one before 2020 at every specification, returns to it in 2020, where the calibration pins it, and then rises toward earnings-related benefits as ageing proceeds, leveling off with population growth. After 2020 the tax rate with the design chosen lies slightly above the one with it pinned, since a more Bismarckian system dissipates less and is worth more to the electorate at the margin, and the Frisch elasticity barely moves either line.Figure OA.12 The design and the tax along the baseline path, U.S.

section: OA.4.5 The timing of the design choice
text:
OA.4.5 The timing of the design choice
Appendix C.1 of the paper shows that each timing of the choice puts the design at a corner when redistribution is costless: a design chosen together with the tax rate re-splits benefits current retirees have already earned, a design chosen one period ahead trades the young’s redistributive stake against the forward-looking one, and a design chosen once and for all enters every channel at once. The table reports the numerical checks of these timings.
\(\cdot\)



One block per timing of the choice, all without the cost of redistribution. Chosen with the tax or one period in advance, the design is the Beveridgean corner at every IES checked. Chosen once and for all, it is the Beveridgean corner at the lower elasticities of the grid shown and the Bismarckian corner at the higher ones; near the switch the electorate is close to indifferent between the two, so the switch is not sharply located.

With the tax: the largest value of the marginal effect of the design on the political objective, an equation in appendix C of the paper, over a grid of \(\theta_t\) on [0,1] and the dates 1990–2170 of the baseline path; it is negative everywhere, so the choice is the corner \(\theta_t = 0\) at every date. Its scale is that of the objective, which differs across \(\rho\); the log case is checked in the regression suite of the code. One period in advance: the design in force in 2020 on the path where the choice binds from the first period. Once and for all: the design chosen in 2020, with the savings of the period before made in anticipation of the vote, and the tax rate at that design. Pinning the savings ratio at the incumbent design instead, an unanticipated vote, gives the same design in every row.

OA.4.6 An alternative cost specification
A cost attached to the design rather than to the transfer it performs. The table sets it beside the paper’s cost, which scales with the dispersion of relative incomes: the calibration of each, and the design each lets the electorate choose under acute ageing and under France’s income distribution and voting patterns.
\(\cdot\)



The paper’s cost in the upper block and the cost on the design in the lower. Under both, acute ageing makes the chosen design more Bismarckian and France’s voting patterns less so at every IES, the first by less and the second by more under the cost on the design. Under the cost on the design, France’s income distribution, which compresses the redistributive stakes but leaves that cost in place, takes the design to the Bismarckian corner at every IES.

title: OA.5 Numerical checks
text:
OA.5.1 Date-specific and stationary policies
Section 4 of the paper computes date-specific Markov policy functions by backward induction along the demographic transition, and selects among the candidate equilibria at each state; the technical documentation (Berg and Gonzalez-Eiras 2026) gives the algorithms and the code. This chapter reports two checks of that computation.
The table prints the gap between the date-specific solution and a time-invariant policy function, the approximation of much of the quantitative politico-economic literature, at the same dates. Section 4 summarizes it in a footnote.
\(\cdot\)

The tax gaps are largest at the lowest IES, in Argentina above all, and every gap shrinks toward zero late in the horizon, apart from the last period shown.

OA.5.2 Equilibrium selection
The table prints, for every file of results behind an exhibit, the largest number of equilibria and of candidate solutions found at any state, and the number of states at which no candidate passed the equilibrium test and the solver fell back on the integral rule of the technical documentation. A single equilibrium at every state means that the selection rule of section 4 never had to choose. A file prints no count where its solve selects no tax, the economic-equilibrium paths, or where its driver did not record the count: the calibration grids of the U.S., the UK and France, the Frisch-elasticity and timing files, and the tax layer of the CRRA endogenous-design calibration and path files, whose design layer is counted in the lower panel. The paper’s statement in section 4 rests on the files that record the count.

The tax rule is the selection of the technical documentation, which falls back on the tax that maximizes its integral criterion where no candidate passes the equilibrium test; a solve that does not select a tax (the economic-equilibrium paths, with taxes held at the baseline path) or did not record its counts leaves them out. The design layer is that of the exact recursion under CRRA preferences, which compares the candidate designs with the retirees’ savings shares held fixed and then makes the shares consistent: its candidates are the brackets of that consistency residual, and where none closes to an equilibrium it falls back on comparing each design at its own consistent shares. escExperiments.csv and escExperimentsUK.csv, which the endogenous-design exhibits read, merge the escShocks* files, whose counts are the rows above.

References
Every table and figure of the paper’s quantitative sections and of this appendix, except the paper’s figure 5.1 of Argentina’s beneficiaries, is produced by the pipeline in python/paper of the repository, in three stages: the calibrations, the experiments, and a build that reads only their results and writes the exhibits in seconds. REPLICATION.md in the repository is the map from data and code to every output, with the commands and the time each stage takes; the technical documentation (Berg and Gonzalez-Eiras 2026) describes the model, its equilibria and the algorithms.
The table lists every exhibit shown here, where it appears and the builder that makes it, with the files it reads; each exhibit’s Source has the same, with downloads and the command that rebuilds it.
